newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: Malaysia frees Timor activists, deports foreigners.
newsitem.headline: Malaysia frees Timor activists, deports foreigners.

text.p: Malaysia on Monday deported the 10 remaining foreigners who came for a short-lived conference on East Timor at the weekend and freed from jail nine other human rights activists and two journalists.

The conference, held before Tuesday's anniversary of the 1991 killing by Indonesian troops of at least 50 demonstrators in East Timor's capital of Dili, was broken up by unruly protesters from a youth group allied to the Malaysian government.

Ten Filipinos were deported on Monday, the Immigration Department said. Thirty-six foreign activists were expelled on Sunday, including two Roman Catholic bishops -- Nobuo Somo of Nagoya, Japan and Hilton Deakin of Melbourne, Australia.

Police on Monday freed eight Malaysians and a Singaporean who took part in the Asia Pacific Conference on East Timor II (APCET II). Asiaweek's correspondent in Kuala Lumpur, Roger Mitton, was also released from jail.

Mitton was detained along with the foreigners, an Australian Broadcasting Corporation reporter, a Malaysian reporter and dozens of local activists after the youth group stormed into Saturday's meeting, breaking down a door, overturning furniture and shouting at participants.
The government had objected to the conference, saying it could damage relations with neighbouring Indonesia.
Singaporean human rights activist Samy Dorai and Malaysian journalist Sonny Imbaraj Krishnan were among the dozen that were released on Monday after two nights in jail.

Krishnan, 37, a journalist for the Nation newspaper in Bangkok said: "It's horrible inside. We were kept in a 10-by-12 foot (three by 3.6 metre) cell together with rapists, murderers and drug addicts."

Krishnan said the detainees were told to report back to the Kuala Lumpur police station on November 23 to hear what charges, if any, were being made against them. By late on Monday, 18 Malaysian activists were still in jail.
Seven youth group demonstrators, who were arrested along with the conference participants, were all released on Saturday. It was not clear if they faced charges.
An APCET II statement on Monday called on the government to release all the detainees and "to differentiate between the aggressors and the victims of violence and to act in fairness".
It also called on the government "not to incite further violence by praising the actions of the rioters".

Deputy Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim said on Sunday the protesters, who belonged to the youth wings of the three main political parties in Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad's ruling coalition "acted on their own. I was not notifed by them."
Ahmad Zahid Hamidi, youth wing leader of Mahathir's United Malays National Organisation, said on Sunday it was he who ordered the youth group to take action to stop the conference.
The presidents of the Malaysian Indian Congress and the Malaysian Chinese Association -- the two other main parties in Mahathir's coalition -- said they endorsed the action.
The opposition leader in Parliament, Lim Kit Siang, said in a statement on Monday the disruption of the conference "was a blot on the human rights record of Malaysia".

"It is obvious from the course of events that the ugly demonstration was orchestrated with the full knowledge of the authorities concerned so as to give a pretext to the government to stop the conference from taking place," he said.
